title: Simulators: Cisco Packet Tracer, GNS3, EVE-NG and Mininet

videos.script: Nobody learns routing by reading about it. You learn it by building a network, breaking it, and watching what the packets do. {{build}} But a rack of routers and switches costs money and space. And one wrong command on a real network takes an office offline. {{rack}} So people practise on networks that live inside a computer, and there are three ways to build one. {{three}} A simulator, like Cisco Packet Tracer, imitates the devices. A program pretends to be a router. {{pt}} An emulator, like GNS3 or EVE-NG, runs the router's real software inside a virtual machine. {{emu}} And tools like Mininet build the network out of the Linux kernel itself, with real interfaces and real packets. {{mininet}} In this lesson you run Mininet. One command builds three switches and three hosts, and every host pings every other one. {{run}} Then you open the lab this whole course runs on, and see what it is made of: namespaces, virtual cables and bridges, all on one machine. {{lab}} By the end you know what each tool is really running, and which one fits the thing you want to practise. {{choose}}
